problem.text: Which of the following expressions is never a prime number when $p$ is a prime number?

steps.title: Where to start: remainders when dividing by 3
steps.body: To show a number is never prime, look for a small factor it always has. Squares behave very neatly when you divide by $3$. Every prime $p$ other than $3$ is not a multiple of $3$, so it leaves remainder $1$ or $2$ when divided by $3$.

your_turn.prompt: Find the remainders when $1^2$, $2^2$, $4^2$ and $5^2$ are divided by $3$. What pattern do you see?
your_turn.answer: $1$, $4$, $16$, $25$ all leave remainder $1$. A number that is not a multiple of $3$ always has a square that leaves remainder $1$.

steps.title: What adding a constant does
steps.body:
So for a prime $p \ne 3$ we can write $p^2 = 3k + 1$ for some whole number $k$. Adding a constant $c$ gives
$$p^2 + c = 3k + (c + 1).$$
If $c + 1$ is a multiple of $3$, then all of $p^2 + c$ is a multiple of $3$. It is also bigger than $3$, so it cannot be prime.

your_turn.prompt: Use this idea on a different expression: can $p^2 + 14$ be prime when $p$ is a prime other than $3$?
your_turn.answer: No. $14 + 1 = 15$ is a multiple of $3$, so $p^2 + 14$ is a multiple of $3$ bigger than $3$.

steps.title: Do not forget p = 3
steps.body: Careful: the remainder argument says nothing about $p = 3$ itself, because $3^2 = 9$ leaves remainder $0$, not $1$. So for any expression you suspect, you must also test $p = 3$ by hand.

your_turn.prompt: Go back to $p^2 + 14$. Is it prime when $p = 3$?
your_turn.answer: $9 + 14 = 23$, which is prime. So $p^2 + 14$ is sometimes prime, even though it fails for every other prime. The $p = 3$ check really matters.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Among $16, 24, 26, 46, 96$, only $26$ has $c + 1 = 27$ a multiple of $3$. So $p^2 + 26$ is not prime for $p \ne 3$, and for $p = 3$ it is $9 + 26 = 35 = 5 \cdot 7$, not prime either. Each other choice is prime for some prime $p$: $5^2 + 16 = 41$, $7^2 + 24 = 73$, $5^2 + 46 = 71$, $19^2 + 96 = 457$. The answer is **(C)**.

wrong_choices.E: $p^2 + 96$ is composite for every prime from $2$ through $17$, so stopping early makes it look right. But $p = 19$ gives $361 + 96 = 457$, which is prime.
